warmup.q: A handler submits two tasks to newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() inside try-with-resources. Task A takes 2 s. Task B throws after 100 ms. The handler calls b.get() first. When does the handler's exception reach its caller?
options: After about 100 ms: b.get() throws, and the executor cancels A
After about 2 s: b.get() throws at 100 ms, but close() waits for A to finish
Never: the executor logs B's exception and returns null
After about 100 ms, and A is still running when the caller sees the exception
warmup.why: get() throws at 100 ms, but leaving the try block runs close(), which waits for every task. Nothing cancels A, so the failed request still takes 2 s. The last option is what happens with a long-lived executor in a field: the method fails fast, and A keeps running with nobody waiting for it.

sections.h: A failed fan-out keeps working after nobody cares
sections.html:
Here is the fan-out from lesson 3 of this track, inside a quote handler. It needs the customer record (a CRM call that takes 2 s on a bad day) and a credit limit check, which fails after 100 ms.

Java
try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    Future<Customer> customer = perTask.submit(() -> crm.find(id));   // up to 2 s
    Future<Limit> limit = perTask.submit(() -> limits.check(id));     // fails at 100 ms
    return new Quote(customer.get(), limit.get());
}
Kotlin
Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask ->
    val customer = perTask.submit(Callable { crm.find(id) })    // up to 2 s
    val limit = perTask.submit(Callable { limits.check(id) })   // fails at 100 ms
    Quote(customer.get(), limit.get())
}

The request is doomed at 100 ms, and it fails at 2 s. customer.get() waits the full 2 s before limit.get() gets to throw. Swap the two get() calls and it still takes 2 s, because close() waits for the CRM call and nothing tells that call to stop.

Many services keep one executor in a field instead. Then the method fails at 100 ms, but the CRM call keeps running with nobody waiting for its answer. It holds an HTTP connection and maybe a semaphore permit. Under load these orphans pile up, and nothing in a thread dump says which request they belonged to.

Three things are missing here:

  • Failure doesn't cancel anything. To stop the siblings you must call cancel(true) on each other future, in every fan-out, on every error path.
  • Lifetimes aren't tied to the code. A Future is a value you can store anywhere, so nothing promises that the threads a method started have ended when it returns.
  • Context doesn't follow the work. A ThreadLocal set by the handler, such as the request id in your logging MDC, is empty in the subtasks. InheritableThreadLocal copies it into every new thread, and the copy goes stale.

Structured concurrency fixes the first two with one rule: subtasks can't outlive the block that started them, the same way a local variable can't outlive its method. Scoped values, at the end of this lesson, fix the third.

try.title: Watch the orphaned call
steps: Read LeakDemo. Variant A opens an executor per request in try-with-resources. Variant B uses one shared executor. For each, predict when the request fails and whether the CRM call finishes.
Run it with the command below.
Fix variant A by hand. Wrap limit.get() in a try, call customer.cancel(true) in the catch (ExecutionException e), then rethrow. Run it again.

code.title: LeakDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.vthreads.l05; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** * A quote handler fans out two calls: a slow CRM lookup (2 s) and a credit-limit check * that fails after 100 ms. Watch what happens to the slow call once the request has failed. */ public class LeakDemo { static volatile long t0; static void log(String what) { System.out.printf("%,7d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, what); } static String customer() throws InterruptedException { try { Thread.sleep(2_000); // the slow CRM call log("customer: call finished, nobody needs the result"); return "ACME Ltd"; } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("customer: interrupted, stopped early"); throw e; } } static String limit() throws InterruptedException { Thread.sleep(100); throw new IllegalStateException("credit limit service: 503"); } // A: an executor per request, in try-with-resources static String quoteA() throws Exception { try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<String> customer = perTask.submit(LeakDemo::customer); Future<String> limit = perTask.submit(LeakDemo::limit); return limit.get() + " " + customer.get(); // throws at 100 ms... } // ...but close() waits for the CRM call } static final ExecutorService SHARED = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); // B: one long-lived executor for the whole service static String quoteB() throws Exception { Future<String> customer = SHARED.submit(LeakDemo::customer); Future<String> limit = SHARED.submit(LeakDemo::limit); return limit.get() + " " + customer.get(); // throws at 100 ms, and returns } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("A: executor per request, closed by try-with-resources"); t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { quoteA(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { log("request failed: " + e.getCause().getMessage()); } System.out.println("B: one shared executor"); t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { quoteB(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { log("request failed: " + e.getCause().getMessage()); } Thread.sleep(2_500); // stay alive to see what B left behind SHARED.close(); } }

alt.title: LeakDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.vthreads.l05 import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** * A quote handler fans out two calls: a slow CRM lookup (2 s) and a credit-limit check * that fails after 100 ms. Watch what happens to the slow call once the request has failed. */ @Volatile private var t0 = 0L private fun log(what: String) = println("%,7d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, what)) private fun customer(): String = try { Thread.sleep(2_000) // the slow CRM call log("customer: call finished, nobody needs the result") "ACME Ltd" } catch (e: InterruptedException) { log("customer: interrupted, stopped early") throw e } private fun limit(): String { Thread.sleep(100) throw IllegalStateException("credit limit service: 503") } // A: an executor per request, closed by use {} private fun quoteA(): String = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> val customer = perTask.submit(Callable { customer() }) val limit = perTask.submit(Callable { limit() }) limit.get() + " " + customer.get() // throws at 100 ms... } // ...but close() waits for the CRM call private val shared = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() // B: one long-lived executor for the whole service private fun quoteB(): String { val customer = shared.submit(Callable { customer() }) val limit = shared.submit(Callable { limit() }) return limit.get() + " " + customer.get() // throws at 100 ms, and returns } fun main() { println("A: executor per request, closed by use {}") t0 = System.nanoTime() try { quoteA() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { log("request failed: ${e.cause?.message}") } println("B: one shared executor") t0 = System.nanoTime() try { quoteB() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { log("request failed: ${e.cause?.message}") } Thread.sleep(2_500) // stay alive to see what B left behind shared.close() }

try.expect: A: the CRM call finishes at about 2,000 ms, and only then does the request fail, although the error was known at 100 ms. B: the request fails at about 100 ms, and the CRM call still finishes at about 2,000 ms, for a request that is long gone. After your fix, A prints customer: interrupted, stopped early and fails at about 100 ms. That fixes one fan-out. Every other fan-out in the service needs the same code on every error path.

sections.h: A scope ties every subtask to one block
sections.html:
A structured scope has three operations, and the code always has the same shape:

Java
try (var scope = new FailFastScope()) {                  // this lesson's lab
    Supplier<Customer> customer = scope.fork(() -> crm.find(id));
    Supplier<Limit> limit = scope.fork(() -> limits.check(id));
    scope.join();                                        // waits, or throws the first failure
    return new Quote(customer.get(), limit.get());
}                                                        // close(): no subtask is still running
Kotlin
FailFastScope().use { scope ->                           // this lesson's lab
    val customer = scope.fork { crm.find(id) }
    val limit = scope.fork { limits.check(id) }
    scope.join()                                         // waits, or throws the first failure
    Quote(customer.get(), limit.get())
}                                                        // close(): no subtask is still running

fork starts a subtask on a new virtual thread. join waits for the subtasks. close is the guarantee: when the block ends, every thread the scope started has ended, whether the block returned, threw or was interrupted. The policy here is fail fast: the first subtask to fail cancels the others, and join throws that failure at once.

You build exactly this in the lab, on a plain newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). Each forked task runs inside a wrapper. If the task throws, the wrapper records the failure with AtomicReference.compareAndSet(null, failure), so only the first one wins, and then cancels everything else. Cancel means interrupt. That stops code blocked in sleep, socket reads, locks and queues, which covers almost all blocking on virtual threads. A loop that computes and never checks the interrupt flag keeps running.

Two details are easy to get wrong, and the tests check both.

The siblings you interrupt fail too, with an InterruptedException. Those failures must not replace the real one. The compare-and-set already handles it, because the real failure got there first.

close() must wait for threads, not for futures. Future.cancel(true) interrupts the thread and marks the future done at once. On JDK 21, newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor counts a task as finished as soon as its future is done, so close() can return while a cancelled task is still in its finally block, writing an audit row or releasing a permit. executor.shutdownNow() interrupts every thread and leaves the futures alone, so close() keeps waiting until each thread has really finished.

That second bug looks right and passes most tests, which is the strongest argument for using the JDK's scope once you can. The figure shows the difference it makes.

sections.h: StructuredTaskScope: the JDK's scope, still preview
sections.html:
StructuredTaskScope is the JDK's version. Its current shape arrived in JDK 25 (JEP 505, the fifth preview). It is still a preview API in JDK 26 (JEP 525) and JDK 27 (JEP 533). JEP 543 makes it final in JDK 28, due in March 2027, with the JDK 27 API unchanged. Until then you need --enable-preview, which is why this course keeps it out of the Gradle labs.

Here is the quote handler in the JDK 25 shape:

Java
Quote quote(String id) throws InterruptedException {
    try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) {           // fail on the first failure
        Subtask<Customer> customer = scope.fork(() -> crm.find(id));
        Subtask<Limit> limit = scope.fork(() -> limits.check(id));
        scope.join();               // JDK 25: throws StructuredTaskScope.FailedException
        return new Quote(customer.get(), limit.get());
    }                               // close(): cancels what is left and waits for it
}
Kotlin
fun quote(id: String): Quote =
    StructuredTaskScope.open<Any>().use { scope ->              // fail on the first failure
        val customer = scope.fork(Callable { crm.find(id) })
        val limit = scope.fork(Callable { limits.check(id) })
        scope.join()               // JDK 25: throws StructuredTaskScope.FailedException
        Quote(customer.get(), limit.get())
    }                              // close(): cancels what is left and waits for it

It is your FailFastScope with stricter rules. Subtasks run on virtual threads. get() before join() throws IllegalStateException. Scopes must nest like blocks, and the JDK checks that you close them in order. A JSON thread dump (jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json) shows each scope's threads grouped under it, so you can see which request a thread belongs to.

The policy is a Joiner that you pass to open. JDK 25 has four:

  • Joiner.awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow(), the default: fail fast, and join() returns null.
  • Joiner.allSuccessfulOrThrow(): fail fast, and join() returns the subtasks as a Stream<Subtask<T>>.
  • Joiner.anySuccessfulResultOrThrow(): the first success wins, and the scope cancels the rest.
  • Joiner.awaitAll(): wait for everything and never throw. You check each subtask's state().

A second argument configures the scope, for example a timeout:

Java
try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.<Rate>anySuccessfulResultOrThrow(),
        cf -> cf.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)))) {
    scope.fork(() -> fxPrimary.rate(pair));
    scope.fork(() -> fxBackup.rate(pair));
    return scope.join();        // the first rate back; the slower call is cancelled
}
Kotlin
StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.anySuccessfulResultOrThrow<Rate>()) { cf ->
    cf.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(300))
}.use { scope ->
    scope.fork(Callable { fxPrimary.rate(pair) })
    scope.fork(Callable { fxBackup.rate(pair) })
    scope.join()               // the first rate back; the slower call is cancelled
}

If the timeout expires first, the scope cancels both calls and join() throws StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException.

Expect small edits when you move JDKs. JDK 26 renamed anySuccessfulResultOrThrow to anySuccessfulOrThrow, and allSuccessfulOrThrow now returns a List<T> of results. In JDK 27 the built-in joiners make join() throw the ordinary checked ExecutionException, like Future.get(), instead of FailedException. Your lab scope already behaves that way. Articles from the JDK 21 era show new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure() and throwIfFailed(). That API is gone and doesn't compile on JDK 25.

try.title: Run the scope on JDK 25
steps: This one needs JDK 25 exactly, because --enable-preview only works for the JDK's own release. Check with java -version. It runs outside Gradle, as a single-file program, from labs/.
Run ScopeDemo and compare its timeline with LeakDemo. Look at the [req-42] on the customer's line: the subtask can read the request's scoped value.
Make limit() return "limit ok" after its sleep instead of throwing. Predict how long the request takes, then run it.

Now open the scope with a timeout: StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow(), cf -> cf.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(500))) (in Kotlin, open(Joiner.awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow<Any>()) { cf -> cf.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)) }). Predict, then run.

code.title: ScopeDemo.java (JDK 25 preview)
code.html: // JDK 25 only. StructuredTaskScope is a preview API in JDK 25 (JEP 505). From labs/: // java --enable-preview --source 25 vthreads/preview/ScopeDemo.java // The quote handler from LeakDemo, written with a scope. Not part of the Gradle build. import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope; import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope.Joiner; // for the Try it import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope.Subtask; public class ScopeDemo { static final ScopedValue<String> REQUEST_ID = ScopedValue.newInstance(); static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String what) { System.out.printf("%,7d ms [%s] %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, REQUEST_ID.orElse("-"), what); } static String customer() throws InterruptedException { try { Thread.sleep(2_000); // the slow CRM call log("customer: call finished"); return "ACME Ltd"; } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("customer: interrupted, stopped early"); throw e; } } static String limit() throws InterruptedException { Thread.sleep(100); throw new IllegalStateException("credit limit service: 503"); } static String quote() throws InterruptedException { try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // default joiner: fail on the first failure Subtask<String> customer = scope.fork(ScopeDemo::customer); Subtask<String> limit = scope.fork(ScopeDemo::limit); scope.join(); // throws FailedException at about 100 ms return limit.get() + " " + customer.get(); } // close(): every subtask has ended } static void handle() { try { log("quote: " + quote()); } catch (StructuredTaskScope.FailedException e) { log("request failed: " + e.getCause().getMessage()); } catch (StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException e) { log("request timed out"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { ScopedValue.where(REQUEST_ID, "req-42").run(ScopeDemo::handle); // subtasks see req-42 too log("done: the binding has ended, and no subtask is still running"); } }

From labs/: // kotlinc vthreads/preview/ScopeDemo.kt -include-runtime -d vthreads/build/scope-demo.jar // java --enable-preview -jar vthreads/build/scope-demo.jar // Not part of the Gradle build. In Kotlin code you would usually use coroutineScope instead. import java.time.Duration import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope.Joiner // for the Try it private val REQUEST_ID: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance() private val t0 = System.nanoTime() private fun log(what: String) = println("%,7d ms [%s] %s".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, REQUEST_ID.orElse("-"), what)) private fun customer(): String = try { Thread.sleep(2_000) // the slow CRM call log("customer: call finished") "ACME Ltd" } catch (e: InterruptedException) { log("customer: interrupted, stopped early") throw e } private fun limit(): String { Thread.sleep(100) throw IllegalStateException("credit limit service: 503") } private fun quote(): String = StructuredTaskScope.open<Any>().use { scope -> // default joiner: fail on the first failure val customer = scope.fork(Callable { customer() }) val limit = scope.fork(Callable { limit() }) scope.join() // throws FailedException at about 100 ms limit.get() + " " + customer.get() } // close(): every subtask has ended private fun handle() { try { log("quote: ${quote()}") } catch (e: StructuredTaskScope.FailedException) { log("request failed: ${e.cause?.message}") } catch (e: StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException) { log("request timed out") } } fun main() { ScopedValue.where(REQUEST_ID, "req-42").run(Runnable { handle() }) // subtasks see req-42 too log("done: the binding has ended, and no subtask is still running") }

try.expect: First run: at about 100 ms the customer line says interrupted, stopped early, then request failed: credit limit service: 503, then the done line, with [-] because the binding has ended. When both succeed, the quote arrives after about 2,000 ms, since the default joiner waits for every subtask. With the 500 ms timeout, the customer is interrupted at about 500 ms and the request reports request timed out. In every case the done line comes last: the scope never leaves a subtask running.

sections.h: Scoped values: request context with a lifetime
sections.html:
Request context (a correlation id, a tenant, the authenticated merchant) travels down the call chain without being a parameter of every method. The usual tool is a ThreadLocal, and it has three problems:

  • It is mutable. Any code can call set(), so the code that reads it can't tell where the value came from.
  • It lives as long as the thread unless someone calls remove(). On a pooled thread, a forgotten value leaks into the next request. That is how one tenant's log lines end up tagged with another tenant's id.
  • Its inheritance is a copy. InheritableThreadLocal copies values into each new thread. With a virtual thread per subtask, that's one copy per subtask, and a change in the parent never reaches the children.

A scoped value is the replacement. It is final in JDK 25 (JEP 506), so it needs no flag. You bind it for the length of one call, everything inside that call can read it, and nobody can change it:

Java
static final ScopedValue<String> TENANT = ScopedValue.newInstance();

void handle(Request req) {
    ScopedValue.where(TENANT, req.tenant()).run(() -> process(req));   // bound only inside run()
}

static String ledgerKey(String account) {
    return TENANT.get() + ":" + account;     // NoSuchElementException if nobody bound it
}
Kotlin
val TENANT: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance()

fun handle(req: Request) {
    ScopedValue.where(TENANT, req.tenant).run(Runnable { process(req) })   // bound only inside run()
}

fun ledgerKey(account: String): String =
    TENANT.get() + ":" + account              // NoSuchElementException if nobody bound it

There is no set(). To use another value for a nested call, bind again with where(...).run(...). The outer value comes back when that call returns. isBound() and orElse(...) let library code handle the case where nothing is bound, and call(...) is the variant that returns a value and may throw.

Scoped values flow into subtasks forked in a StructuredTaskScope. The child doesn't get a copy. It reads the parent's binding, which is safe because the binding can't change and the scope ends before the binding does. They do not flow into threads you start yourself or into executor tasks, so pass the value as an argument there.

On JDK 25 that gives a clear split. Use scoped values for new request context today. Their flow into subtasks needs StructuredTaskScope, which is still preview. Keep ThreadLocal where a library requires it, like SLF4J's MDC, and clear it in a finally.

try.title: ThreadLocal and ScopedValue side by side
steps: You need JDK 25 or later. Scoped values are final there, so this runs without --enable-preview.
Read ScopedValueDemo and predict its six lines of output before you run it.
Run it. Then, in part 1, move the work into a try and add TENANT_TL.remove() in a finally. Run it again.

code.title: ScopedValueDemo.java (JDK 25)
code.html: // JDK 25 or later. Scoped values are final in JDK 25 (JEP 506), so no flag is needed. From labs/: // java vthreads/preview/ScopedValueDemo.java // Not part of the Gradle build, because the labs compile for JDK 21, where ScopedValue is a preview API. import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class ScopedValueDemo { static final ThreadLocal<String> TENANT_TL = new ThreadLocal<>(); static final ScopedValue<String> TENANT = ScopedValue.newInstance(); // deep in the call chain: reads the context, never sets it static String ledgerLookup() { return "ThreadLocal=" + TENANT_TL.get() + ", ScopedValue=" + TENANT.orElse("unbound"); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { // 1. a ThreadLocal set on a pooled thread and never removed try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1)) { pool.submit(() -> { TENANT_TL.set("bank-a"); // forgot TENANT_TL.remove() return ledgerLookup(); }).get(); System.out.println("1. next task, same pool thread: " + pool.submit(ScopedValueDemo::ledgerLookup).get()); } // 2. a scoped value is bound for one call, and gone afterwards ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-a").run(() -> System.out.println("2. inside run(): " + ledgerLookup())); System.out.println(" after run(): " + ledgerLookup()); // 3. rebind for a nested call; the outer binding comes back when it returns ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-a").run(() -> { ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-b").run(() -> System.out.println("3. nested: " + ledgerLookup())); System.out.println(" outer again: " + ledgerLookup()); }); // 4. a thread you start yourself does not inherit the binding ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-a").run(() -> { Thread child = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> System.out.println("4. plain thread: " + ledgerLookup())); try { child.join(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); } }

alt.title: ScopedValueDemo.kt (JDK 25)
alt.html: // JDK 25 or later. Scoped values are final in JDK 25 (JEP 506). Needs the Kotlin command-line // compiler. From labs/: // kotlinc vthreads/preview/ScopedValueDemo.kt -include-runtime -d vthreads/build/sv-demo.jar // java -jar vthreads/build/sv-demo.jar // Not part of the Gradle build, because the labs compile for JDK 21, where ScopedValue is a preview API. import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.Executors private val TENANT_TL = ThreadLocal<String>() private val TENANT: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance() // deep in the call chain: reads the context, never sets it private fun ledgerLookup() = "ThreadLocal=${TENANT_TL.get()}, ScopedValue=${TENANT.orElse("unbound")}" fun main() { // 1. a ThreadLocal set on a pooled thread and never removed Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1).use { pool -> pool.submit(Callable { TENANT_TL.set("bank-a") // forgot TENANT_TL.remove() ledgerLookup() }).get() println("1. next task, same pool thread: " + pool.submit(Callable { ledgerLookup() }).get()) } // 2. a scoped value is bound for one call, and gone afterwards // Runnable { } is optional; it shows this is the carrier's run, not Kotlin's run {} ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-a").run(Runnable { println("2. inside run(): " + ledgerLookup()) }) println(" after run(): " + ledgerLookup()) // 3. rebind for a nested call; the outer binding comes back when it returns ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-a").run(Runnable { ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-b").run(Runnable { println("3. nested: " + ledgerLookup()) }) println(" outer again: " + ledgerLookup()) }) // 4. a thread you start yourself does not inherit the binding ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-a").run(Runnable { val child = Thread.ofVirtual().start { println("4. plain thread: " + ledgerLookup()) } child.join() }) }

try.expect: Line 1 shows ThreadLocal=bank-a in a task that never set it: the value leaked from the previous task on the same pool thread. After your fix it shows ThreadLocal=null. The scoped value is bank-a inside run() and unbound after it, bank-b in the nested call and bank-a again after it. The plain virtual thread prints unbound, because only StructuredTaskScope forks see the parent's binding.

analogy: A structured scope works like a function call for concurrent work. A local variable can't outlive the method that declared it, and a subtask can't outlive the block that forked it. A ThreadLocal is a whiteboard on the thread's wall: anyone can write on it, nobody has to wipe it, and the next person to use the room reads whatever was left. A scoped value is a sealed envelope handed down the call chain and shredded when the call returns. The analogy breaks for subtasks: a scope's forks don't get their own envelopes, they all read the parent's. That is safe only because nobody can change the envelope and the scope ends before the call does.
world: A quote or authorization endpoint in a Quarkus service often fans out to a CRM, a limits service and an FX provider. Today those calls usually go through CompletableFuture or an injected executor, and a failure in one leaves the others running and holding connections. On JDK 25 you can get fail-fast behavior now with a small scope like the lab's, and move to StructuredTaskScope when JDK 28 makes it final. The same rule fits a Temporal activity that fans out: when Temporal cancels or times out the activity, a scope makes sure its HTTP calls stop with it instead of finishing in the background. For context, look at your MDC: SLF4J's MDC is a ThreadLocal, so log lines written inside forked subtasks lose the correlation id unless you copy it in, and a pooled thread that skips MDC.clear() tags the next request with the wrong id.
mistake: The most common mistake is copying StructuredTaskScope code written for a different JDK. new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure() with join().throwIfFailed() is the JDK 21 to 24 API and doesn't compile on JDK 25. JDK 25 code that catches FailedException stops compiling on JDK 27, where join() throws ExecutionException. And --enable-preview only works with the JDK's own release, so a preview API ties the whole build to one JDK version. Pin the JDK version in any code that uses the preview, and keep that code small and in one place. For production services on JDK 25, use a plain executor with explicit cancellation (or a small scope like the lab's), and switch to the JDK's scope when JDK 28 makes it final.

compare.title: Request context that follows the subtasks

java.title: Java: ScopedValue plus a scope (JDK 25, scope in preview)
java.html: static final ScopedValue<String> TENANT = ScopedValue.newInstance(); // final in JDK 25 Statement statement(Request req) throws Exception { return ScopedValue.where(TENANT, req.tenant()).call(() -> { // bound for this call try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // preview in JDK 25 Subtask<Customer> customer = scope.fork(() -> crm.find(req.customerId())); Subtask<Balance> balance = scope.fork(() -> ledger.balance(ledgerKey(req.account()))); scope.join(); return new Statement(customer.get(), balance.get()); } }); } static String ledgerKey(String account) { return TENANT.get() + ":" + account; // the fork reads the parent's binding }

kotlin.title: Kotlin: a coroutine context element
kotlin.html: // the coroutine carries the context, not the thread class Tenant(val id: String) : AbstractCoroutineContextElement(Tenant) { companion object Key : CoroutineContext.Key<Tenant> } suspend fun statement(req: Request): Statement = withContext(Tenant(req.tenant)) { // bound for this block val customer = async { crm.find(req.customerId) } val balance = async { ledger.balance(ledgerKey(req.account)) } // children inherit the context Statement(customer.await(), balance.await()) } suspend fun ledgerKey(account: String): String = (currentCoroutineContext()[Tenant]?.id ?: error("no tenant")) + ":" + account

compare.note: Both are immutable context that children inherit and that ends with the block. The difference is what carries it. A scoped value is bound to a thread's call stack, and only StructuredTaskScope forks inherit it. A coroutine context element is bound to the coroutine, so it survives a coroutine moving to another thread at a suspension point, and every child started with launch or async inherits it. That is why scoped values and ThreadLocals are the wrong tool inside suspending code: a coroutine can resume on a different thread, where the binding isn't there. In Kotlin coroutine code, put context in the coroutine context. Use ScopedValue from Kotlin only in plain blocking code on threads.

worked.title: Make an authorization fan-out fail fast

steps.say: An authorization needs a fraud score and the card's open-to-buy amount. Both are blocking HTTP calls. The code runs on a shared executor field, and the request id lives in a ThreadLocal for logging. Read it and list what goes wrong when the fraud call fails.
steps.code: Auth authorize(Payment p) throws Exception { REQUEST_ID.set(p.requestId()); // a ThreadLocal Future<Score> fraud = shared.submit(() -> fraudApi.score(p)); // 300 ms Future<Money> open = shared.submit(() -> cards.openToBuy(p)); // 80 ms return decide(fraud.get(), open.get()); }

alt.html: fun authorize(p: Payment): Auth { REQUEST_ID.set(p.requestId) // a ThreadLocal val fraud = shared.submit(Callable { fraudApi.score(p) }) // 300 ms val open = shared.submit(Callable { cards.openToBuy(p) }) // 80 ms return decide(fraud.get(), open.get()) }

steps.say: Three problems. If the card call fails, fraud.get() still waits up to 300 ms first. If the fraud call fails, the card call keeps running after authorize has thrown. And both subtasks log without the request id, because REQUEST_ID is set on the handler's thread only. On a pooled handler thread it is also never cleared.

On JDK 25 without preview, use a scope that owns its threads, like the lab's FailFastScope, and pass the request id as an argument. Every subtask now ends before authorize returns, and the first failure cancels the other call.
steps.code: Auth authorize(Payment p) throws Exception { try (var scope = new FailFastScope()) { // 1. open: owns the subtasks String rid = p.requestId(); // 2. context as a plain argument Supplier<Score> fraud = scope.fork(() -> fraudApi.score(p, rid)); Supplier<Money> open = scope.fork(() -> cards.openToBuy(p, rid)); scope.join(); // 3. first failure cancels the other return decide(fraud.get(), open.get()); } // 4. close: nothing left running }

alt.html: fun authorize(p: Payment): Auth = FailFastScope().use { scope -> // 1. open: owns the subtasks val rid = p.requestId // 2. context as a plain argument val fraud = scope.fork { fraudApi.score(p, rid) } val open = scope.fork { cards.openToBuy(p, rid) } scope.join() // 3. first failure cancels the other decide(fraud.get(), open.get()) } // 4. close: nothing left running

steps.say: On JDK 25 with --enable-preview, the JDK's scope does the same job, and a scoped value carries the request id into both forks. No method signature has to change.
steps.code: static final ScopedValue<String> REQUEST_ID = ScopedValue.newInstance(); Auth authorize(Payment p) throws Exception { return ScopedValue.where(REQUEST_ID, p.requestId()).call(() -> { // 1. bind the context try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // 2. fail-fast scope Subtask<Score> fraud = scope.fork(() -> fraudApi.score(p)); // forks read REQUEST_ID Subtask<Money> open = scope.fork(() -> cards.openToBuy(p)); scope.join(); // 3. FailedException on JDK 25 return decide(fraud.get(), open.get()); } // 4. close: nothing left running }); }

alt.html: val REQUEST_ID: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance() fun authorize(p: Payment): Auth = ScopedValue.where(REQUEST_ID, p.requestId).call<Auth, Exception> { // 1. bind the context StructuredTaskScope.open<Any>().use { scope -> // 2. fail-fast scope val fraud = scope.fork(Callable { fraudApi.score(p) }) // forks read REQUEST_ID val open = scope.fork(Callable { cards.openToBuy(p) }) scope.join() // 3. FailedException on JDK 25 decide(fraud.get(), open.get()) } // 4. close: nothing left running }

steps.say: When you move to JDK 27 or 28, change the error handling where you call authorize: catch ExecutionException from join() instead of StructuredTaskScope.FailedException. The fork, join and close lines stay the same.

lab.title: Build a fail-fast scope on an executor
steps: Run the tests once. All seven fail with UnsupportedOperationException. Read the class comment in FailFastScope: it lists the rules the tests check.

Add the state as fields: an ExecutorService from Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), a CopyOnWriteArrayList<Future<?>>, an AtomicReference<Throwable> for the first failure and a volatile boolean joined.

Write fork. Submit a Callable that runs task.call() in a try. In the catch, record the failure with compareAndSet(null, failure); if that wins, call executor.shutdownNow() to interrupt the siblings. Rethrow. Add the future to the list and return a Supplier that throws IllegalStateException until join() has run, then returns future.resultNow().
Handle a fork after cancellation: once the executor is shut down, submit throws RejectedExecutionException. Catch it and return a handle whose get() always throws IllegalStateException.

Write join: call get() on each future in order, ignore ExecutionException and CancellationException, and stop as soon as a failure is recorded. Set joined, then throw new ExecutionException(failure) if there was one. Write close: shutdownNow(), then close() on the executor.
Run the tests until all seven pass, then run them twice more.
hints: Why compareAndSet? The siblings you interrupt fail too, with InterruptedException. They fail after the real failure is recorded, so their compareAndSet(null, ...) returns false and they don't replace it.

Don't cancel with future.cancel(true). A cancelled future counts as done at once, and on JDK 21 the executor then stops waiting for that thread while its finally block still runs. The close() test catches exactly that. shutdownNow() interrupts the threads and leaves the futures alone.
catch (Throwable failure) { ...; throw failure; } compiles inside the submitted lambda: Java's precise rethrow knows task.call() can only throw an Exception.
Future.resultNow() (JDK 19 and later) returns the result of a task that succeeded and throws IllegalStateException for one that failed or was cancelled, which is what a handle needs after join().
lab.done: All seven tests in FailFastScopeTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Write the JDK 25 scope from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write Quote quote(String id) that loads a customer and a credit limit at the same time with StructuredTaskScope (JDK 25 preview), fails fast, and closes cleanly. Then write the catch clause a caller needs on JDK 25, and the one it needs on JDK 27.

answer.html: Quote quote(String id) throws InterruptedException { try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // default: fail on the first failure Subtask<Customer> customer = scope.fork(() -> crm.find(id)); Subtask<Limit> limit = scope.fork(() -> limits.check(id)); scope.join(); // throws if a subtask failed return new Quote(customer.get(), limit.get()); // get() only after join() } // close() waits for every subtask } // a caller on JDK 25 try { return quote(id); } catch (StructuredTaskScope.FailedException e) { // unchecked; the cause is the subtask's exception throw new QuoteUnavailableException(e.getCause()); } // on JDK 27 and later, join() throws the checked ExecutionException instead: // } catch (ExecutionException e) { throw new QuoteUnavailableException(e.getCause()); }

alt.html: fun quote(id: String): Quote = StructuredTaskScope.open<Any>().use { scope -> // default: fail on the first failure val customer = scope.fork(Callable { crm.find(id) }) val limit = scope.fork(Callable { limits.check(id) }) scope.join() // throws if a subtask failed Quote(customer.get(), limit.get()) // get() only after join() } // close() waits for every subtask // a caller on JDK 25 try { return quote(id) } catch (e: StructuredTaskScope.FailedException) { // the cause is the subtask's exception throw QuoteUnavailableException(e.cause) } // on JDK 27 and later, catch ExecutionException instead: // } catch (e: ExecutionException) { throw QuoteUnavailableException(e.cause) }

recap: An executor fan-out doesn't cancel the other tasks when one fails, and with a shared executor they outlive the request.
Structured concurrency ties subtasks to a block: fork, join, and a close that guarantees every subtask has ended.
Fail fast means the first failure interrupts the siblings and join() throws it. Built by hand, close() must wait for the threads, not for the futures.
StructuredTaskScope is preview in JDK 25 to 27: open(), a Joiner and FailedException in 25, ExecutionException from JDK 27. JDK 28 makes it final.
Scoped values are final in JDK 25: bound for one call with where(...).run(...), read-only, gone afterwards, and inherited only by StructuredTaskScope forks.
A ThreadLocal used for context is mutable, leaks on pooled threads without remove(), and is copied by InheritableThreadLocal.

explain.prompt: A colleague says that try-with-resources around newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() already gives you structured concurrency. Explain what it gives you, what it is missing, and what StructuredTaskScope and scoped values add.
explain.answer: It gives you half of it. When the block ends, close() waits for every task, so no task outlives the method. What it lacks is a failure policy: when one task fails, nothing cancels the others, so a failed request still waits for the slowest call, and you must write cancel calls on every error path yourself. Hand-built cancellation also has traps, such as close() not waiting for a task you cancelled with cancel(true). StructuredTaskScope adds the policy (the first failure cancels the siblings, or another Joiner such as first success wins), timeouts, and checks that scopes nest properly, and its close() always waits for the threads. It is still preview until JDK 28. Scoped values, final in JDK 25, add context that flows into the scope's subtasks without copying, can't be changed by callees, and disappears when the call ends, unlike a ThreadLocal.

deeper.html:
Custom joiners. A Joiner has two hooks, onFork and onComplete, and a result() method that join() calls at the end. onComplete returns true to cancel the scope. That is enough for policies the built-in joiners don't cover, such as "stop once three of five ledger replicas agree" or "collect successes and ignore failures". onComplete runs on the thread of the subtask that just finished, so a joiner's state must be thread-safe. Check the Javadoc of the exact JDK you use, because JDK 26 changed the hook signatures slightly.

Why CompletableFuture doesn't solve this. allOf waits for everything even after one future fails, and cancel(true) on a CompletableFuture doesn't interrupt the thread doing the work: it only completes the future. The lesson "CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out" builds fan-out that way; notice how much code its error handling needs compared with a scope.

Kotlin already has this. In coroutine code, coroutineScope { async { } } gives the same guarantees without a preview flag: children can't outlive the scope, the first failure cancels the siblings, and cancellation reaches each child at its next suspension point. The coroutines track covers it. StructuredTaskScope matters most for Java code and for Kotlin code that blocks on threads.

Scoped values and virtual threads. A ThreadLocal costs a map entry per thread, and with a million virtual threads that adds up, as lesson 4 of this track showed. A scoped value binding is attached to the call, not copied per thread, and its forks share it. That makes it the natural fit for one virtual thread per request with many short subtasks.

Old articles. Before JDK 25 the API was StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure and ShutdownOnSuccess, subclasses you created with new. Scoped values had static helpers such as ScopedValue.runWhere, which were removed during the previews. If a snippet uses either, it was written for an older preview.
